content:
I tried to change the IMAP server address for an existing T-bird account

Don't change an existing account. Create a new account for the new server.

T-bird and/or my ISP deleted the saved password and IMAP server line for that account in T-bird's Saved Passwords table, so T-bird cannot get incoming E-mails.

When this is an existing account, you'll have to authenticate once, and tell Thunderbird to remember the password. It will then be stored in Tools -> Options -> Privacy & Security -> Passwords -> Saved Passwords.

If this is an account using OAuth2 authentication, Thunderbird will only remember an authentication token, and not the actual account password.

In any case, you'll have to enter your account password once to regain access to the account. If you forgot the password, check with your email provider about password reset options.

content:
Not AFAIK, as feature of Tbird (don't know why). Maybe some mozilla addon does this? Or 3rd party app. Technically, if someone w/ any computer savvy can access a device's storage (locally, remotely), they can grab stored email or data, w/out opening the client (e.g., Tbird), then read it somewhere else.

Not an expert here, but only way I've read to prevent this, is to encrypt the email data, so it has to be decrypted w/ a PW before can be read (whether data is copied at the device, or DL remotely by hackers).

Often requires creating a separate partition. Possibly other "container" to encrypt. Commonly done in Linux distros. Several acclaimed, open source encryption apps (for 'Nix). Maybe for Win.

Data partition often has to be decrypted, before the app using the data is launched, so data is readable, where it's expected. Or may be able to put the app (Tbird) & data on same encrypted partition & decrypt both at same time. Lots of people encrypt their entire 'home' partition (in 'Nix) where many of user's personal files, data are stored.

It's not that hard (in Linux). Probably possible in Win, but I haven't used it in years.
